label: Saturation versus audible distortion — what it changes
non_processing_alternatives: Rebalance the source.
Change the arrangement or sound selection.
Use compression or automation if the main problem is level movement.
Check level and loudness bias before processing.
Check the source, performance, timing, arrangement, and masking context.
problem_or_outcome: Saturation is a degree and shape of nonlinear distortion, not a completely separate physical process; the useful distinction is subtle enrichment versus clearly audible waveform reshaping.
recommended_first_experiment: Build a clean listening reference: Level-match a barely audible drive setting against a deliberately obvious one, then choose the least amount that creates the intended density in context.
stop_rule: Stop once you can reliably judge added density, softened peaks, and improved audibility without losing articulation or depth. Back off or undo immediately if louder output can masquerade as warmth, while excess drive can flatten contrast and create grit.
tradeoffs: Louder output can masquerade as warmth, while excess drive can flatten contrast and create grit.
A louder or peak-reduced version can seem better before the actual timbral or envelope change is judged.
A local improvement can create a new masking, headroom, phase, noise, or arrangement problem.
undo: Bypass the processor and restore the saved input, output, mix, timing, and routing values; if a duplicate or parallel path was created, mute or remove it.
what_to_listen_for: added density, softened peaks, and improved audibility without losing articulation or depth
why_it_may_help: Saturation is a degree and shape of nonlinear distortion, not a completely separate physical process; the useful distinction is subtle enrichment versus clearly audible waveform reshaping.

label: Even and odd harmonic emphasis — what it changes
non_processing_alternatives: Adjust EQ or source tone.
Choose a different performance or instrument.
Check level and loudness bias before processing.
Check the source, performance, timing, arrangement, and masking context.
problem_or_outcome: Even-versus-odd language is a useful orientation, but real processors generate level- and frequency-dependent mixtures; judge the whole transfer behavior rather than choosing from a slogan.
recommended_first_experiment: Build a clean listening reference: Compare two processors at matched loudness using the same modest input level, then focus on midrange density, edge, and low-frequency stability.
stop_rule: Stop once you can reliably judge whether one version adds body while the other adds edge, and whether the effect changes with note level. label: Waveshaping and transfer curves — what it changes
non_processing_alternatives: Fix clipping upstream.
Use a cleaner gain stage.
Check level and loudness bias before processing.
Check the source, performance, timing, arrangement, and masking context.
problem_or_outcome: A nonlinear transfer curve maps input amplitude to output amplitude, so input gain is part of the sound and the same plug-in can behave very differently at different levels.
recommended_first_experiment: Build a clean listening reference: Send a fixed phrase through three input levels while compensating output, then compare the onset of coloration and peak flattening.
stop_rule: Stop once you can reliably judge where coloration begins, whether low notes modulate upper content, and how transients change. Back off or undo immediately if changing input gain without matching output makes it impossible to separate tone from loudness.
tradeoffs: Changing input gain without matching output makes it impossible to separate tone from loudness.
A louder or peak-reduced version can seem better before the actual timbral or envelope change is judged.
A local improvement can create a new masking, headroom, phase, noise, or arrangement problem.

label: Harmonic density versus noise and hiss — what it changes
non_processing_alternatives: Improve the recording environment.
Edit or automate noise between phrases.
Use targeted EQ.
Check level and loudness bias before processing.
Check the source, performance, timing, arrangement, and masking context.
problem_or_outcome: Nonlinear processing can raise low-level ambience and make existing noise more obvious even when it is not generating broadband noise itself.
recommended_first_experiment: Build a clean listening reference: Compare the processor on a phrase and on the gap before it at matched output, then listen separately to signal tone and noise-floor change.

label: Level-dependent coloration — what it changes
non_processing_alternatives: Improve performance consistency.
Use automation or compression.
Check level and loudness bias before processing.
Check the source, performance, timing, arrangement, and masking context.
problem_or_outcome: Because nonlinear coloration rises with amplitude, a dynamic source can receive little effect on quiet notes and heavy distortion on peaks.
recommended_first_experiment: Build a clean listening reference: Use clip gain or a controlled input trim to feed two comparable phrases more consistently, then level-match the output and compare tone.
stop_rule: Stop once you can reliably judge whether quiet and loud phrases keep a coherent character while preserving musical dynamics. Back off or undo immediately if pre-leveling can over-smooth an expressive performance, while leaving peaks uncontrolled can produce harsh bursts.
tradeoffs: Pre-leveling can over-smooth an expressive performance, while leaving peaks uncontrolled can produce harsh bursts.
A louder or peak-reduced version can seem better before the actual timbral or envelope change is judged.
A local improvement can create a new masking, headroom, phase, noise, or arrangement problem.

why_it_may_help: Because nonlinear coloration rises with amplitude, a dynamic source can receive little effect on quiet notes and heavy distortion on peaks.

label: Input drive versus output trim — what it changes
non_processing_alternatives: Change the fader balance.
Use region gain or automation.
Check level and loudness bias before processing.
Check the source, performance, timing, arrangement, and masking context.
problem_or_outcome: Input gain determines how hard the nonlinear stage is driven; output trim should be used to remove loudness bias, not to undo the distortion itself.
recommended_first_experiment: Build a clean listening reference: Set a low and moderate drive, compensate each output to the bypassed level, and compare in the full mix.
stop_rule: Stop once you can reliably judge tone, peak shape, sustain, and clarity after loudness is neutralized. Back off or undo immediately if an unmatched output can make almost any distortion setting seem more exciting.
tradeoffs: An unmatched output can make almost any distortion setting seem more exciting.
A louder or peak-reduced version can seem better before the actual timbral or envelope change is judged.
A local improvement can create a new masking, headroom, phase, noise, or arrangement problem.

label: Kick-drum clipping — what it changes

label: Transient versus sustain — what it changes
